title: Bushfires did not cause the post-1997 runoff loss in south-east Australia: unburned catchments lost 8-14% of predicted runoff, and fire raised runoff for up to 9 years (175 CAMELS-AUS catchments)
abstract: Question: is the persistent post-1997 runoff deficit in south-east Australia (SE-AU) caused by bushfire and forest regrowth, a cause that earlier campaign work did not test? Approach: 175 SE-AU catchments (CAMELS-AUS v2.03; annual tables of bundle 871b2192), residuals from per-catchment 1951-1996 fits of runoff on rain, previous-year rain and temperature (AGCD and SILO rain), and Geoscience Australia Historical Bushfire Boundaries v2.0 rasterized at 250 m. Planned tests: deficit of unburned and burned catchments, a panel model with catchment and year effects and time-since-wildfire terms, and the deficit after removal of fire terms. Results: the 47 catchments with less than 5% burned in 1980-2021 lost 13.7% (1997-2009) and 11.9% (2010-2021) of predicted runoff with AGCD and 13.0% and 8.0% with SILO. The 32 catchments with no dated wildfire lost 9-13% (32-40 mm per year). Catchments with 30% or more burned did not have a larger deficit (difference -0.7 points in 2010-2021, 95% CI -11.9 to +9.4). Fire increased runoff: a fully burned catchment had +31% of mean flow in years 0-1 (CI 19-39%), +20% in years 2-4 and +11% in years 5-9; later terms were -5% to -6% and uncertain. The early terms stayed positive in 14 post hoc variants that control for the dry years before fires, and in a permutation test (p <= 0.003). Thus fire offset about 9-14% of the deficit; without fire terms the 2010-2021 deficit was 16.0% (AGCD) and 8.5% (SILO). In a post hoc forward test, the 2019-20 fires raised 2020-2021 runoff by 6-13% of mean flow, one third to one half of the predicted 22%. Limitations: fire extents without severity, incomplete NSW dates, annual linear models, records to 2021, post hoc robustness analyses. The cause of the SE-AU deficit remains unknown, but it acts in unburned catchments.
